passage: Cognitive psychologists distinguish two common ways of studying for a later test: rereading the assigned material and self-testing by repeatedly trying to recall it from memory. A researcher proposes that the very act of retrieving information during self-testing, rather than the mere additional exposure to the material that self-testing also happens to provide, is what actually strengthens memory over the long term.
question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's proposal?

choices.text: Students who reread their material reported feeling noticeably more confident about it than students who tested themselves on it.
Students who self-tested ended up spending more total time studying the material than students who only reread it.
Students who recalled the material on a practice test remembered more of it a week later than students who spent the same amount of time rereading it.
Students ended up performing noticeably better on the later test when they were allowed to keep the original study material in front of them the whole time they were answering.

explanation: The correct answer is C. The proposal is that retrieval itself, not the extra exposure self-testing happens to give, strengthens memory. A finding that students who retrieved the material remembered more a week later than students who reread it for the same amount of time isolates retrieval by holding exposure time equal—exactly what the proposal needs. Choice A concerns confidence rather than retention. Choice B introduces a difference in study time, which confounds the comparison rather than supporting the retrieval claim. Choice D describes open-book performance, which does not bear on the value of recall.

_meta.anchor: Testing effect; retrieval vs. mere exposure as the source of better retention
